abstract: Nitrogen (N) form acquired by plants reflects both physiological preference and environmentally mediated availability. Hydroponic controlled-environment agriculture (CEA) removes many constraints governing N availability yet remains predominantly reliant on nitrate (NO3-) nutrition. We used differential 15N stable-isotope labeling to quantify ammonium (NH4+) and NO3- acquisition by four lettuce (Lactuca sativa L.) cultivars grown hydroponically under terrestrial ambient (410 ppm) and spaceflight-relevant elevated (3000 ppm) CO2. Plants received equivalent concentrations of NH4+ and NO3-, with either N form selectively enriched with 15N during the final 24 h of growth. All cultivars exhibited significantly greater shoot 15N enrichment following 15NH4+ than 15NO3- labeling under both CO2 environments, demonstrating consistent preferential NH4+ acquisition. Preference magnitude varied among cultivars and broadly corresponded with biomass and total shoot N accumulation, driven predominantly by increased NH4+-derived enrichment rather than reduced NO3--derived enrichment. Elevated CO2 did not significantly alter N-form preference, although strong NH4+ preference persisted at 3000 ppm. These findings distinguish physiological acquisition preference from environmentally mediated N availability and provide a basis for reconsidering nitrate-dominant nutrition in terrestrial and space CEA, including integration with recycled reduced N.
